aStandoffInsteadOfAWar41.title: A War Fought Without the United States
aStandoffInsteadOfAWar41.situation: Speculative: Pearl Harbor never happens. Without the attack that united American opinion overnight in the real war, Congress stays as divided as before the embargo: isolationists argue that a Pacific war is Britain's and China's problem, and interventionists cannot force a declaration for a country nobody has attacked. Japan's Southern Operation goes ahead anyway, taking Malaya, the Indies and the Philippines, an American territory now under occupation, without American entry into the war. China's war, already four years old, goes on as brutally as before with no American ally committed to ending it.

choices.label: Press for a declaration of war regardless: the occupation of American territory in the Philippines is provocation enough

advisor.name: Stimson
advisor.position: Congress does not need a second Pearl Harbor to see that the first already happened, and American soil is occupied, which is not something to treat as insufficient.

choices.outcome: A harder argument than Stimson had to make in the real war, since the emotional unity Pearl Harbor gave overnight is not available. The occupation of the Philippines is a casus belli on paper, American territory under foreign military occupation, but turning it into a declaration against a Congress still having the same argument as in November is a slower and more contested fight.

choices.label: Accept the standoff: focus entirely on the war against Germany, leave the Pacific to Britain, China, and the Dutch

advisor.name: Marshall
advisor.position: Europe First was always the plan even with Pearl Harbor forcing the Pacific, and without that forcing there is no reason to fight a second war the country was never attacked into.

choices.outcome: Speculative. Europe First, which was one front among several in the real war, becomes the whole American war. Every division, ship and dollar of Lend-Lease goes to Britain and the Soviet Union, undiluted by a Pacific commitment. What that leaves China, Britain's Asian colonies and the Dutch East Indies to face alone against an unchecked Japan is the next chapter's question.

theSlowerDeclaration42.title: Five Weeks in 1917, and No Guarantee of the Same Now
theSlowerDeclaration42.situation: Speculative. The precedent for how quickly outrage turns into a declaration is the Zimmermann Telegram: published on March 1, 1917, confirmed by Zimmermann himself two days later, and still five weeks before Congress declared war, over a threat that reached toward the American mainland. The occupation of the Philippines is real, but it lacks the instant clarity Pearl Harbor supplied and the direct threat to the mainland that the 1917 case had. Congress has to be walked to war, not shocked into it, and walking takes a case built one senator at a time.

choices.label: Build the case methodically: hearings, documented atrocity reports from the occupied Philippines, a slow accumulation of pressure

advisor.name: Stimson
advisor.position: Zimmermann took five weeks against a threat aimed at Texas, and a threat aimed at an American colony is not going to move Congress faster because the Secretary wants it to.

choices.outcome: The case builds as the 1917 case did, through hearings and documented reports and not a single galvanizing morning, and it takes longer than five weeks because the provocation is harder to sell than a threat to Texas. When the declaration comes it rests on accumulated pressure and not on shock, a slower fuse but, once lit, as real.

choices.label: Force the vote early: accept a chance of losing it rather than let the case build indefinitely

advisor.name: Marshall
advisor.position: Each week the argument builds is a week the Philippines spends further consolidated under occupation, and it is better to force a vote that might be lost than win a stronger case for a country with nothing left worth declaring war to recover.

uncertain.title: The early vote passes
uncertain.outcome: Speculative. The vote passes by a narrower margin than the 1917 vote, converting a case still being built into a declaration before isolationist resistance can organize.

uncertain.title: The early vote fails
uncertain.outcome: The likelier outcome. The vote fails, and forcing it early costs the case its momentum. Congress does not return to where it was: a failed declaration is a signal in itself, and isolationists treat it as confirmation and not as a setback.

choices.outcome: A modeled alternative. Forcing an early vote risks losing the argument permanently instead of winning it more slowly, on the theory that Japan's consolidation of the Philippines is a clock this Congress cannot ignore while it deliberates.

warBeginsLate42.title: A War Congress Chose Rather Than Had Chosen For It
warBeginsLate42.situation: Speculative. The declaration passes. Unlike the real war, entered in one unified morning, this one comes after months of hearings and atrocity reports, a Congress walked to the vote and not shocked into it. What it authorizes, how quickly American forces mobilize for a Pacific theater nobody planned for in advance, and what Japan's resource area can withstand after however long unopposed, is not yet written.

choices.label: Close the file here: the declaration itself was the question worth asking

advisor.name: Marshall
advisor.position: The question was whether Congress could be walked to a war it was not shocked into, and it could, and what that war looks like is a different question from the one this file was opened to answer.

choices.outcome: Speculative. A stopping point: the declaration, and how differently it arrives without Pearl Harbor, is the counterfactual this thread set out to test. What the war itself looks like against a Japan that had months or years to consolidate is open.

choices.label: Follow it forward: build the war this declaration actually produces, not just the declaration itself

advisor.name: Stimson
advisor.position: The effort went into proving Congress could be walked to a vote and not shocked into one, and the next question is what kind of war that walk bought, not only that it reached the door.

choices.outcome: Speculative. The thread stays open. What Japan's resource area looks like after a year or more unopposed, and what American force arrives to contest it once the declaration passes, is territory this thread now goes looking for.

japanUnopposed43.title: The Tide's High-Water Mark
japanUnopposed43.situation: Speculative. Intelligence reaching Washington, thin and secondhand for want of any American combat presence in the theater, describes an argument inside Imperial General Headquarters over whether to press further, linking a push through Burma toward India with a renewed southern advance, or to consolidate. The debate is real. So are the constraints that limited Japan's reach in the real war: an oil-dependent economy, a merchant fleet already strained supplying the empire, and the cost of partisan resistance in Malaya, the Philippines and China. Whether an unopposed Japan has room to expand or is meeting the same logistics ceiling as in the real war, Washington has almost no way to verify.

choices.label: Treat the expansionist reports as the more credible reading: an unopposed Japan probably does have room to press further

advisor.name: Marshall
advisor.position: An enemy with no one shooting at it has room its logistics do not obviously deny it yet, and it is better to plan for that room being real than to assume Japan's restraint where no American forces are in place to test it.

choices.outcome: Speculative. Washington reads Japan's internal debate as evidence of capability and not only ambition, and plans around an empire that may still be expanding. It is an anxious posture, and the intelligence gap cannot resolve it from here.

choices.label: Treat the logistics constraints as the more credible reading: an unopposed Japan is likely finding its own ceiling regardless

advisor.name: King
advisor.position: Nobody's oil reserves grow because nobody is shooting at their tankers, and the absence of an American fleet does not change what Japan can fuel.

choices.outcome: Speculative. The skeptical reading, and the better grounded: Japan's real economy strained under its conquests even with an American war degrading it, and there is no reason an unopposed empire's oil and shipping arithmetic should work out better. It cannot be tested from here, because the forces that would confirm it are not in the theater.

warWithoutAmerica45.title: Manchuria, Not Hiroshima
warWithoutAmerica45.situation: Speculative. Germany is defeated on about the real calendar, perhaps a little early, given two years of Lend-Lease that never had to share its weight with a Pacific war. Stalin's commitment at Yalta to enter the Pacific war within months of Germany's fall was motivated by Soviet claims on Manchuria, southern Sakhalin and the Kurils and not by any obligation to Washington, so it holds. The Red Army crosses into Manchuria and collapses the Kwantung Army in about a week, as in the real war. No atomic bomb is used: the Manhattan Project went ahead, but a bomb built against Germany has no Japanese city to fall on when America is not at war with Japan. Japan's government, watching its strongest field army collapse in days, must find its own way forward without the shock that ended the argument in its war cabinet in the real war. Washington watches from as far outside as the standoff has kept it from the start.

choices.label: Maintain the standoff to its logical end: let Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and the Dutch settle Japan's fate and the postwar Pacific without an American voice in the room

advisor.name: Marshall
advisor.position: The position was chosen four years ago, its becoming uncomfortable is no reason to abandon it now, and if the principle was worth holding in 1941 it is worth holding at the finish.

choices.outcome: Speculative. A position held for four years is held to the end: no declaration, no aid beyond the choices made along this path, and no American voice in the settlement that the Soviet Union, Britain, China and the Dutch reach over a defeated Japan. The cost is a postwar Pacific order shaped entirely by the powers that fought for a say in it, while the country that chose not to fight has little claim to one.

choices.label: Break the standoff at the finish: engage diplomatically now, before a postwar settlement gets decided entirely without American input

advisor.name: Hull
advisor.position: The principle held for four years is worth keeping, but not through the one conversation that decides what the Pacific looks like for the next fifty years, because consistency is different from a country talking itself out of a seat at its own century.

choices.outcome: Speculative. A late reversal, inconsistent with four years of non-engagement: Washington re-enters the conversation at the moment it stops being free and becomes consequential. Whether four years of absence earned any credibility, or whether a seat at the table has to be won by the fighting this country chose not to do, is a question the postwar settlement answers.

internmentQuestion42.title: Executive Order 9066
internmentQuestion42.situation: General DeWitt's Western Defense Command is pressing for the forced removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast, citing a security threat that his own command's later reporting cannot substantiate with actual evidence of sabotage or espionage. Attorney General Biddle and the Justice Department are pushing back hard, warning that mass removal without individualized evidence sets a precedent no wartime necessity requires. Roughly two-thirds of the roughly 120,000 people who would be affected are American citizens by birth. This is not a battlefield decision, but it is one this command's own domestic security posture has to answer for.

choices.label: Authorize the removal: approve Executive Order 9066 as DeWitt's command has requested

advisor.name: Stimson
advisor.position: General DeWitt has offered conviction that the risk exists and not evidence of it, but the Secretary of War will not overrule the commander on the coast in wartime, and the order should proceed.

choices.outcome: Roughly 120,000 people of Japanese descent, most of them American citizens, are forcibly removed from the West Coast and held in inland camps for the duration of the war, on the basis of a military necessity claim later government reviews concluded was not supported by the evidence available at the time. No comparable order is issued against German or Italian Americans. The Supreme Court upholds the order in Korematsu v. United States in 1944; the conviction is not formally repudiated until decades later.

choices.label: Reject the removal order: side with the Justice Department's objection, pursue individualized security review instead

advisor.name: Biddle
advisor.position: The position will be called soft on security in a war still being lost on every front that matters, and it is also true that the evidence for this measure does not exist and it should not be authorized on conviction alone.

choices.outcome: A modeled alternative: the position Justice Department officials held and lost. Individual review of specific, credible suspicions, and not of an entire ethnic population regardless of citizenship, was an option in early 1942, and it is how German and Italian nationals in the United States were mostly handled. It spares the injustice the real order caused. It does not remove the wartime anxiety DeWitt's command was responding to.

choices.label: Restrict the order to Issei non-citizens only, exempting American-born Nisei citizens from removal

advisor.name: Biddle
advisor.position: The government's legal authority under the Alien Enemies Act reaches non-citizens and not citizens by birth, and a narrower order can be defended on that ground but this one cannot.

choices.outcome: A modeled alternative on the distinction the Alien Enemies Act draws between non-citizens and citizens by birth, which DeWitt's order did not honor. It still removes and detains a large population under wartime enemy-alien authority, on firmer legal ground, and spares the two-thirds who were American citizens. It resolves the order's clearest constitutional problem and not the anxiety behind it.

doolittleRaidAllied42.title: Doolittle's Gamble
doolittleRaidAllied42.situation: Sixteen Army B-25s under Lieutenant Colonel Doolittle are aboard Hornet, escorted by Enterprise, closing on Japan for the first strike on the home islands of the war, a mission built on a thin margin: the bombers can't land back aboard the carriers, so the plan depends on launching close enough to reach airfields in China after the raid, but not so close that Hornet is spotted first. A Japanese picket boat has just sighted the task force roughly two hundred miles further out than the plan called for, radioing a warning before it's sunk. Doolittle's crews now have fuel for the bombing run itself, but not for the airfields in China the original plan assumed.

choices.label: Launch immediately despite the shortened range: accept that most crews will have to ditch or bail out over China

advisor.name: Halsey
advisor.position: The task force has been spotted and every hour of waiting brings Japanese carriers closer to finding it first, so the bombers should launch now and the fuel math be left to Doolittle's people.

choices.outcome: All sixteen aircraft reach Japan, but none reaches the intended Chinese airfields: most crews bail out or crash-land along the Chinese coast, eight are captured by the Japanese, three are executed and one dies in captivity, and the raid kills few people and destroys little. The effect on morale is out of proportion to the damage: after four months of unbroken defeats the American public has its first good headline, and in Imperial Headquarters the raid silences the Naval General Staff's remaining doubts about Midway. It also triggers a Japanese reprisal campaign through Zhejiang and Jiangxi, the provinces that sheltered the raid's other crews, which kills Chinese civilians in numbers never precisely counted, estimated from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand.

choices.label: Abort the mission: the fuel margin no longer supports it, preserve the aircrews and the carriers

advisor.name: Doolittle
advisor.position: Months went into the mission and its own leader asks to cancel it, preferring to explain a cancelled raid to Washington to explaining sixteen crews lost over open ocean.

choices.outcome: A modeled alternative: aborting, which Doolittle and Halsey had the authority to choose and did not. Cancelling preserves the aircrews and denies Japan the embarrassment that hardened the case for Midway, but it also denies a tired home front its first good news of the Pacific war. Whether Midway happens on the same schedule without the raid's shock is answered on the Japan side. The choice also avoids the reprisal campaign against the Chinese provinces that sheltered the crews, a civilian death toll never precisely counted.

theBatBombQuestion43.title: Project X-Ray: A Dentist's Idea, Sixteen Months Later
theBatBombQuestion43.situation: The proposal reached Roosevelt's desk in January 1942: a letter from a Pennsylvania dentist, Lytle Adams, about bats, incendiaries and Japan's wooden cities, forwarded to the War Department with a note in the President's hand, 'this man is not a nut.' Sixteen months of funded Army development later, the idea has data behind it. A standard incendiary load starts an estimated 167 to 400 fires, and the same weight in bat-carried incendiaries, released before dawn so the animals roost in attics and eaves, is projected at 3,600 to 4,700. The program has also burned down part of an Army airfield in New Mexico, when armed bats escaped a test enclosure and roosted under a fuel tank. The program needs a decision: push it toward combat readiness, or put the resources elsewhere.

choices.label: Push it toward combat readiness: transfer the program to the Navy, fund it at the scale its own fire-efficiency numbers justify

advisor.name: King
advisor.position: On paper the bat bomb is a better weapon than what is being dropped now, and the transfer is authorized on that basis alone and not out of confidence that bats are a serious instrument of war.

choices.outcome: What happened. The Navy takes the program and passes it to the Marine Corps, and testing continues through 1943 and into 1944 with results that keep supporting the fire-efficiency case. The timeline does not improve. In 1944, with about two million dollars spent and combat readiness projected for mid-1945 at the earliest, the program is cancelled on the orders of Admiral King, the officer who authorized the transfer.

choices.label: Redirect the resources now: the fire-efficiency numbers are real, but this staff has higher-confidence programs competing for the same funding

advisor.name: Nimitz
advisor.position: The numbers are not doubted on paper, but a weapon built from live animals that must be captured, refrigerated and kept cold enough to stay dormant carries a great deal of operational fragility for a fire-efficiency advantage.

choices.outcome: A modeled alternative. The redirection comes about a year earlier than the real cancellation, on the logic King later used himself: a weapon made of live, hibernating, individually caged animals is harder to schedule than the fire-efficiency numbers suggest. About two million dollars stay unspent on a project that produced impressive test results and no combat use.

bismarckSea43.title: The Bismarck Sea
bismarckSea43.situation: A Japanese convoy of eight transports and eight destroyers, carrying roughly 6,900 troops to reinforce New Guinea, is spotted running the Bismarck Sea without air cover adequate to the threat. Fifth Air Force has spent months developing low-altitude skip-bombing tactics specifically against ships like these, and General Kenney is proposing to commit the full weight of that doctrine against a single convoy rather than holding it in reserve for a larger target.

choices.label: Commit the full weight of skip-bombing doctrine against the convoy, all available bombers in a single, coordinated strike

advisor.name: Kenney
advisor.position: The air force has practiced this attack for months against a target it did not have, it has one now, and the doctrine should not be held in reserve for a convoy that may not be this exposed again.

choices.outcome: Every transport and half the destroyer escort are sunk, and roughly 3,000 Japanese soldiers die, most before ever reaching New Guinea, in what becomes one of the most lopsided air-versus-naval engagements of the entire war. Japan effectively stops attempting daylight convoy reinforcement of New Guinea by sea afterward, a doctrine shift as consequential as the battle's own casualty count: the skip-bombing tactics developed against exactly this kind of target close off an entire category of resupply for the rest of the campaign.

choices.label: Hold back part of the strike force in reserve, in case a larger or more critical target appears later

advisor.name: MacArthur
advisor.position: A guaranteed result today has real appeal, but a better target tomorrow is not worth letting a real one finish crossing the water today.

choices.outcome: A modeled alternative. Part of the strike force is held back against a target that never appears so clearly again. More of the convoy reaches New Guinea than in the real battle, which gives Japan's defense of the island reinforcements it did not have, and daylight convoys are not shown to be suicidal in the way the full strike showed. Japan's high command draws a less certain lesson from a less total defeat.

yamamotoSurvives43.title: Yamamoto's Silence
yamamotoSurvives43.situation: Speculative. Yamamoto is still alive and commanding Combined Fleet, and by every signal fleet intelligence can read he still holds the position he has held since before Pearl Harbor: Japan's only chance was a war fast enough to end before American production caught up, and the window is closing. Fleet intelligence has just shown that it can identify one officer's flight plan to the minute, and that the source survives a decision not to use it. Nimitz's staff has to decide whether that restraint was the right lesson or only the safe one.

choices.label: Keep the same discipline: treat the decrypts as too valuable to spend on tactical opportunities, however good

advisor.name: Layton
advisor.position: The source has now been shown to survive restraint, and it may not survive appetite.

choices.outcome: Speculative. A policy and not a single decision: the decrypts stay reserved for strategic warning, convoy routing and fleet movements, and not for individual officers, for the rest of the war. Whatever tactical chances that discipline leaves behind are never counted, because a target never struck appears in no after-action report. The source itself is never seriously endangered by this fleet's use of it.

choices.label: Loosen the restriction: this fleet just proved the source can survive being used. Use it again when it matters

advisor.name: Nimitz
advisor.position: The restriction held once and the secret survived, and the next two years should not be spent being careful out of habit and not judgment.

uncertain.title: The looser standard pays off without costing the source
uncertain.outcome: Speculative. The gamble that held once holds again: intelligence is used more freely against real opportunities through the rest of 1943, and Japan's communications discipline does not improve in response. The fear in the fleet's intelligence staff turns out to have been the more cautious reading of a risk that never materialized.

uncertain.title: A closer call than the first time
uncertain.outcome: Speculative. The source is not blown, but it is a closer call. A change in Japanese naval codes later in 1943, unrelated in cause, costs weeks of readable traffic, and the intelligence staff spends those weeks unsure whether the change was routine or a response to the pattern of use they had argued against.

choices.outcome: Speculative. The fleet treats the source as resilient and not fragile, betting that April's restraint was a caution this war cannot afford twice.

theTarawaQuestion43.title: The Tarawa Question
theTarawaQuestion43.situation: Word of Tarawa's cost reaches Washington before the smoke has cleared: more than a thousand Marines dead in seventy-six hours on an island smaller than Central Park, with photographs of bodies in the surf released to the press. Congress wants to know whether every atoll between here and Tokyo will cost the same, and the direct-assault doctrine that produced Tarawa is on trial, whether or not anyone in the room says so.

choices.label: Defend the doctrine publicly: argue that bypassing costs more blood in the long run than paying it up front

advisor.name: Holland Smith
advisor.position: The doctrine's cost will not be apologized for, and each time Congress needs to hear it, the answer is what letting a fortified position sit behind the lines costs instead.

uncertain.title: The doctrine survives the hearing
uncertain.outcome: The doctrine holds. Congress keeps asking questions, but no directive changes what the Joint Chiefs may order, and the Central Pacific advance keeps its direct-assault option for whatever comes next.

uncertain.title: Washington overrules the theater command
uncertain.outcome: Speculative, and the rarer outcome. Political pressure over Tarawa's casualties forces a formal review that ties the theater command's hands on future direct assaults, whatever Holland Smith or the Joint Chiefs judge militarily. Every later island campaign is fought under a bombardment requirement imposed by politics and not tactics.

choices.outcome: A defense on the tactical logic Holland Smith and other advocates of direct assault held: a bypassed fortress is a fortress you fight later, on its terms, with less warning. Whether that survives a Congress looking at casualty photographs is open.

choices.label: Adjust doctrine: extend preparatory bombardment before future assaults, even at the cost of tempo

advisor.name: Nimitz
advisor.position: Tarawa's naval gunfire schedule was too short, the after-action report says so, and what it says should be fixed before anyone has to ask.

choices.outcome: Longer, heavier preparatory bombardment ahead of future assaults, a tactical lesson from Tarawa's after-action reports and not a concession to public opinion. It costs tempo that the real schedule did not spend.

macArthurTension44.title: MacArthur Goes to the Press
macArthurTension44.situation: MacArthur has again gone around the chain of command through friendly press contacts, presenting the Navy's leapfrogging strategy as an abandonment of loyal Filipinos left under occupation while the fleet bypasses them for faster objectives. It is effective and sympathetic, and it breaches unified command. The Joint Chiefs have tolerated this from him for two years, and whether they keep tolerating it is an open question.

choices.label: Let it stand: MacArthur's popularity and the Philippines' symbolic weight make this a fight not worth having

advisor.name: Marshall
advisor.position: Officers have been relieved for less than this, but the one man whose removal the newspapers would make the story instead of the war will not be relieved.

choices.outcome: What happened, more or less, for the rest of the war. MacArthur keeps making the argument publicly, the Joint Chiefs keep working around him privately, and the Philippines campaign proceeds under his command essentially as history recorded it.

choices.label: Relieve him for insubordination: unified command discipline matters more than one theater commander's popularity

advisor.name: King
advisor.position: A public relations campaign against agreed strategy has been tolerated for two years because relieving him seemed more trouble than it was worth, and it was never going to stop being worth it less.

choices.outcome: Speculative. The fight nobody in Washington wanted finally happens. MacArthur is relieved, seven years before Truman relieved him in Korea in the real war, and Southwest Pacific Area command needs someone new by the end of the week.

macArthurAftermath44.title: Eichelberger's Command
macArthurAftermath44.situation: Speculative. Robert Eichelberger, MacArthur's subordinate and the general who took Buna when headquarters was demanding results the front could not deliver, inherits Southwest Pacific Area command. He has none of MacArthur's political weight or instinct for headlines, and the Philippines campaign he inherits was planned around a personality this command no longer has.

choices.label: Keep the Philippines liberation plan intact: honor the commitment MacArthur made publicly, under new command

advisor.name: Eichelberger
advisor.position: The promise was not his to make alone and is not another man's to break because he is gone, and the liberation plan should be finished as it was begun.

choices.outcome: Speculative. The campaign proceeds on schedule under a competent and much less famous general who never gets a photograph of his own wading ashore on Leyte, because there is no MacArthur left to stage one.

choices.label: Reconsider the Philippines timetable on its military merits alone, without a personal promise to honor

advisor.name: Nimitz
advisor.position: The Philippines timetable should be decided on where the airfields and shipping are, and not on a pledge a relieved commander made to newsreel cameras.

choices.outcome: Speculative. Freed from the political weight of MacArthur's public promise, Pacific strategy is reassessed on Nimitz's terms: whether Formosa serves the fleet better than Luzon. The debate that MacArthur won in the real war by persistence is settled by staff study instead, and staff studies do not always come out where the persistent man would have pushed them.

stilwellPreserved44.title: Stilwell's Narrower Command
stilwellPreserved44.situation: Speculative. Hurley's week produced a document and not a resolution: Chiang will accept Stilwell in command of Chinese forces in Burma and Yunnan only. It is less than Stilwell wanted and more than the real breakdown left him. Command in China's interior, and of the Nationalist divisions facing Ichi-Go, stays with Chiang's generals. Ichi-Go itself is already overrunning airfields on its own timetable, and this negotiation was never in a position to stop it.

choices.label: Accept the narrower command as the real, achievable outcome, rather than reopen the fight for more

advisor.name: Marshall
advisor.position: Asking for everything cost a great deal last time, and it is better to keep the general than win an argument about how much of China he commands.

choices.outcome: Speculative. Stilwell stays in China, in a role smaller than the ultimatum asked for and larger than the real recall left him, which was none. Whether a general who stays inside China achieves more than he could from Washington is uncertain. Ichi-Go's outcome barely moves, since it was a problem of divisions and supply that no negotiation in Chungking could fix.

choices.label: Push again for the fuller command the original ultimatum demanded, betting the narrower deal is a first step, not a ceiling

advisor.name: Stilwell
advisor.position: Two and a half years in the theater were not spent to command Yunnan, and the ultimatum should be put again for what the war requires.

choices.outcome: Speculative. The second ask lands as the version Hurley's week was meant to prevent. Chiang reads it as Washington going back on a settlement made weeks before, and reaches for the same demand for Stilwell's recall. Stilwell leaves China regardless, on a slightly different date and after a slightly different argument, having spent the extra month proving Hurley's instinct right.

kyotoTargetDebate45.title: The City Groves Wanted Most
kyotoTargetDebate45.situation: The Target Committee's ranking puts Kyoto first: over a million people, a population and building stock largely untouched by the firebombing that has gutted other candidate cities, which by the committee's logic makes it the clearest test of what the weapon does. Secretary of War Stimson has objected to Groves repeatedly since May. Kyoto was Japan's imperial capital for over a thousand years and remains its religious and cultural center, and Stimson believes that destroying it would poison any postwar relationship the occupation will need. By Stimson's account, it is the only targeting decision in which President Truman personally took part.

choices.label: Back Stimson: strike Kyoto from the list permanently, over Groves' operational objection

advisor.name: Stimson
advisor.position: The Secretary has told General Arnold there is one city he does not touch without direct permission, meant it before the list existed and means it now.

choices.outcome: Truman backs Stimson's objection, the only target-list decision in which he takes part. Kyoto is struck from consideration for good. The remaining candidates are cities the firebombing campaign has not leveled. What is left to decide is which of them, and what warning, if any, they get.

choices.label: Overrule Stimson: retain Kyoto as the primary target, on Groves' argument that its intact population is exactly the point

advisor.name: Groves
advisor.position: Kyoto is large enough that there would be no question about what the weapon does, and that is not a reason to look away but the reason to choose it.

choices.outcome: Speculative. Groves's argument wins on its own logic: a larger, less damaged city makes a clearer demonstration of what the weapon does, and a clearer demonstration is treated as worth more than what Stimson was trying to protect.

kyotoStruck45.title: Stimson's Warning, Ignored
kyotoStruck45.situation: Speculative. The weapon that struck Hiroshima in the real war strikes Kyoto instead: a city with a larger population than Hiroshima's, left deliberately untouched by the firebombing, so the toll runs higher than the real first strike by most estimates. Lost with the people are a thousand years of temples, shrines and archives with no second copy anywhere. Stimson's fear that this loss would poison the occupation is no longer a prediction. It is the condition the occupation has to work in.

choices.label: Make cultural preservation and restoration an explicit occupation priority, as a direct answer to what was destroyed

advisor.name: Stimson
advisor.position: The Secretary said preservation would be the position afterward, did not expect to be the one drafting the policy that has to answer for it, and will not draft it halfheartedly.

choices.outcome: Speculative. An attempt to answer a loss that has no answer: occupation policy makes the United States explicitly responsible for protecting the Japanese cultural and religious sites that survive, shaped by what Kyoto's absence leaves behind. Whether such a commitment means anything to a population that saw the alternative is a question the policy can state an intention about and cannot settle.

choices.label: Proceed with standard occupation policy: treat this as a wartime decision like any other, not a special case requiring one

advisor.name: Groves
advisor.position: The weapon did what weapons of war do, and the occupation needs no special policy to answer for a target selection already defended on its own terms.

choices.outcome: Speculative. The occupation proceeds on the footing it would have had whichever city was struck first, treating Stimson's fear as one more wartime cost and not as a condition needing its own answer. Whether the occupied country reads that as consistency or as indifference is not something policy documents can decide.

targetSelection45.title: The Remaining List
targetSelection45.situation: With Kyoto struck from the target list, the committee's remaining candidates are Hiroshima, Kokura, Niigata and Nagasaki, cities largely untouched by the conventional bombing campaign, chosen partly so that the bomb's effects could be measured against an intact baseline. Leaflets warning of intensified bombing have been dropped over dozens of Japanese cities in general terms. The question now is whether to warn these specific cities by name before a weapon this different arrives.

choices.label: Decline specific warnings: preserve surprise, rely on the general leaflet campaign already underway

advisor.name: Groves
advisor.position: A named warning gives the target city time to move anti-aircraft assets and disperse what the blast is to be measured against, which costs the mission, and the general knows what it costs the people living there.

choices.outcome: What happened, up to this point. No city-specific warning is given beyond the general leaflets already dropped over much of Japan. The remaining question, whether one strike or more than one, isn't decided by this choice.

choices.label: Drop specific warnings naming the candidate target cities, accepting the military cost for the chance to reduce civilian deaths

advisor.name: Stimson
advisor.position: A named warning costs the mission its measurement value, but the Secretary is less certain than General Groves that the measurement is worth what withholding the warning costs the people living in whichever city it turns out to be.

choices.outcome: A modeled alternative: a warning some civilian officials privately favored and lost the argument for. Named warnings risk what Groves predicted, dispersed civilians, moved defenses and a target that is no longer a clean baseline. Whether it saves lives depends on how seriously a population numbed by months of firebombing warnings takes one more leaflet.

hiroshima45.title: Hiroshima
hiroshima45.situation: The Enola Gay drops the first atomic weapon used in war over Hiroshima at 8:15 in the morning. Estimates of the dead vary: about 70,000 to 80,000 killed at once, and between 90,000 and 166,000 by the end of 1945. Under the order of July 25, use of the weapon against the approved target list was authorized as further bombs became available, with no requirement to seek a new decision before each one. Unless someone intervenes, a second strike is already under way by the order already signed.

choices.label: Let the standing order continue: no new decision required, the second weapon proceeds on schedule

advisor.name: Groves
advisor.position: The standing order already covers this, and no new signature is needed to do what the President has authorized.

choices.outcome: No new authorization is sought or given, because none is required. The second bomb goes ahead on the existing order, a decision that in the strictest sense nobody ever makes, and that is only left unmade until it is carried out.

choices.label: Intervene now: pause the order and require the President's own fresh decision before any second strike

advisor.name: McCloy
advisor.position: As written, the order means the next bomb happens because nobody stopped it and not because anybody decided it, and those are not the same thing.

choices.outcome: Speculative. In the real war Truman halted further atomic bombing on August 10, one day after Nagasaki. Here the order pauses a few days earlier, and what follows is on a timeline nobody in Washington has mapped.

nagasaki45.title: Nagasaki
nagasaki45.situation: The primary target, Kokura, is hidden by cloud and industrial haze when Bockscar arrives, and the crew, short of fuel after three passes, goes on to the secondary target. Nagasaki is bombed at 11:02 on a decision made in the air by a flight crew, not at a planning table in Washington. Estimates of the dead run similarly wide to Hiroshima's, roughly 40,000 killed outright and a comparable further toll from injuries and radiation over the following months. The same day, the Soviet Union's declaration of war reaches Tokyo. Japan's Big Six war council meets that night in the Emperor's presence and deadlocks three to three on whether to surrender at all.

choices.label: Make no public statement beyond confirming the strike: let the military record speak for itself

advisor.name: Truman
advisor.position: Everything that needed saying was said after the first bomb, and there is no second speech that says anything different.

choices.outcome: What happened. No separate presidential address follows Nagasaki as one followed Hiroshima. The next decision facing Washington concerns what the government says, and does not say, about what the bombing did to the people under it.

choices.label: Address the public directly again: acknowledge the second strike and its scale honestly

advisor.name: Stimson
advisor.position: Silence after the second bomb reads as something the government is unwilling to own, and it is better to account for it plainly than let the absence of an account do the talking.

choices.outcome: A modeled alternative: a more forthcoming public posture than the government took, while the war's ending is still unresolved in Tokyo. Whether candor now makes it easier to handle honestly what happened to the people of both cities in the months afterward is a separate question.

indianapolisSinking45.title: The Indianapolis
indianapolisSinking45.situation: Having delivered components of the atomic bomb to Tinian, the cruiser Indianapolis is torpedoed by a Japanese submarine on July 30 and sinks in twelve minutes. About 300 of her crew go down with the ship. Roughly 900 are left in open water, and the ship's failure to arrive at her next port goes unreported for four days: several stations logged that she was overdue and none followed up, a failure spread across enough desks that no single person's negligence explains it. When rescue aircraft find survivors by chance, fewer than 320 are alive. Captain McVay survives, and the Navy has to decide how this is answered.

choices.label: Court-martial Captain McVay for failing to zigzag his ship in submarine waters

advisor.name: King
advisor.position: A captain lost his ship, and awareness of what else went wrong that night does not by itself answer whether his own decisions were sound.

choices.outcome: McVay is court-martialed and convicted, the only U.S. Navy captain court-martialed for losing his ship to enemy action in the entire war, despite the Japanese submarine commander who sank him testifying that zigzagging would have made no difference at that range. The routing failures that left the survivors in the water for four days are never formally answered with anything close to the same scrutiny.

choices.label: Order a full review of the reporting failure instead: the four days in the water are the scandal

advisor.name: Nimitz
advisor.position: The failure is less one captain's zigzag pattern than how a ship of that size goes missing for four days without anyone at any station connecting what each was separately told.

choices.outcome: A modeled alternative: a reckoning aimed at the chain of failures and not at the man left holding the ship. Whether a review this late in the war produces reforms that prevent a four-day gap before the fighting ends is the next question.
